1
INTRODUCTION
The government asks this Court to overturn a three decades-long status quo. 
That request should be denied. Since at least 1992, the Federal Bureau of Prisons 
(“BOP”) has treated people diagnosed with gender dysphoria with hormone therapy. 
For over thirty years—from 1992 to 2025—BOP policy has been to continue providing
hormone treatment for people who entered custody already receiving such care. During 
that period, BOP has also expanded access to care, including by initiating hormone 
therapy for people when clinically indicated and by providing accommodations to 
enable social transition (dressing and otherwise living consistently with one’s gender 
identity).
But in 2025, BOP abruptly reversed course and banned such care altogether,
after President Trump signed an executive order barring the use of federal funds for
“any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s 
appearance to that of the opposite sex.” Exec. Order No. 14168, Defending Women from 
Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government
§ 4(c), 90 Fed. Reg. 8615, 8617 (Jan. 20, 2025) (“EO”). To implement the EO, BOP 
overrode its own medical providers’ clinical judgment and mandated the cessation of 
treatment for almost 1,000 people in its custody. 
The district court preliminarily enjoined BOP from enforcing its written policy 
implementing the EO, Program Statement 5260.01, App.8a (the “Program 
Statement”), concluding that the policy is likely arbitrary and capricious. Applying 
settled Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”) precedents, the district court held that

2
the Program Statement violates the APA in three independent but related ways.
First, the Program Statement is arbitrary and capricious because BOP changed 
its position without examining the highly “relevant data” of its own decades-long
experience providing the very healthcare that the Program Statement now prohibits.
Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of the U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 
29, 43 (1983). BOP asserts that it decided to stop providing hormone therapy and social 
transition accommodations because it concluded that this care is not medically 
necessary and poses security and administrative issues. But the administrative record
is silent about BOP’s extensive experience providing this care and whether it supports 
these stated rationales. It is devoid of any evidence indicating whether BOP healthcare 
providers found this care effective, ineffective, or harmful to patients. Nor does the 
record indicate whether any security issues resulted from the provision of this care. 
Wholly ignoring its many years of experience providing this care is the opposite of a
“reasoned explanation” that is “needed for disregarding facts and circumstances that 
underlay or were engendered by the prior policy.” Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 
579 U.S. 211, 221–22 (2016) (quoting FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 
502, 516 (2009)).
Second, the Program Statement is arbitrary and capricious because it is
unreasonable. By “fail[ing] to offer [a] rational connection between facts and 
judgment,” Motor Vehicle Mfrs., 463 U.S. at 56, the Program Statement is not the 
product of “reasoned decisionmaking,” id. at 52. BOP cut off treatment that its 
healthcare providers had recommended for decades and replaced it with

3
psychotherapy—which its own expert acknowledges is backed by no evidence 
demonstrating its efficacy as a treatment for gender dysphoria—and psychotropic 
medications—which BOP’s Medical Director does not even claim treat gender 
dysphoria, only co-existing conditions. Nor does the assertion of security and 
administration concerns constitute a reasonable basis for rescinding this care given 
that BOP has not pointed to a single security incident relating to its provision of this 
treatment over the past 30 years, and it does not ban other types of medical care that 
actually do present security issues.
Lastly, the Program Statement is arbitrary and capricious because the 
government’s stated rationales are pretextual. Dep’t of Com. v. New York, 588 U.S. 752, 
780 (2019). The BOP’s decision to reverse decades-long policy based on an
administrative record that lacks key evidence relevant to its stated rationales gives 
rise to the inference that the agency’s purported reasons were not its actual reasons 
for the policy change. Had BOP’s doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to 
patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP 
would have mentioned it in the administrative record. That glaring omission, as well 
as the unreasonableness of its decision, make it clear that the rationales were contrived 
to support the demand President Trump made in the EO. Where “evidence tells a story 
that does not match the explanation” given for a decision, the government violates the 
APA. Id. at 784.
The government offers no compelling defense of the agency’s errors. For the most 
part, the government repackages arguments that failed to persuade the district court

4
and which received no support at the D.C. Circuit—not from the majority that denied 
the stay request, nor from Judge Walker, who did not endorse the government’s defense 
of the Program Statement’s reasonableness in his dissent. 
Perhaps for this reason, the government’s application advances a new 
contention—one not raised in its stay motion to the district court—asserting that the 
preliminary injunction does not comply with the Prison Litigation Reform Act
(“PLRA”). The government forfeited this argument by failing to raise it below. In any 
event, this argument is meritless. As the district court correctly noted, the relief
complies with the PLRA and extends no further than necessary.
The government fares no better on the remaining stay factors. It has failed to 
demonstrate irreparable harm absent a stay. The government did not appeal an earlier 
injunction preventing it from implementing the EO over a year ago, never claimed 
irreparable harm in its stay motion to the district court, and has failed to show how it 
would be harmed by continuing to provide the treatment that its own doctors 
recommend for patients. 
In stark contrast, Respondents, who are named plaintiffs representing all those
in BOP custody with gender dysphoria (the “Class”), face a significant risk of serious 
harm if their treatment is cut off. This care, which BOP’s healthcare providers have 
determined is clinically appropriate for them, has been provided to Class members for 
years, sometimes even decades. Withdrawing care will cause significant changes to 
their bodies and put Respondents and Class members at serious risk of worsening 
gender dysphoria as well as other mental health symptoms including depression,

5
anxiety, self-harm, and suicidality. Respondents have already experienced some of 
these harms when BOP temporarily discontinued their treatment and they justifiably
fear such harm will recur if this care is again taken away. The equities and public 
interest thus decisively weigh against a stay.
Finally, the government comes to this Court seeking relief not because there is 
an important legal question that warrants this Court’s review but because it is 
dissatisfied with the district court’s application of longstanding legal standards to the 
facts of this case. That is not a basis to intervene in this interlocutory posture.
The Court should maintain the status quo and deny the government’s request 
for a stay that would permit BOP to withdraw Respondents’ and Class members’ 
treatment while the case proceeds.
STATEMENT
I. BOP’S HISTORY OF TREATMENT OF GENDER DYSPHORIA 
For over three decades, BOP has treated people diagnosed with gender 
dysphoria with hormone therapy.1 See, e.g. Cuoco v. Quinlan, No. 91-7279, 1992 WL 
350755, at *4 (S.D.N.Y. Nov. 16, 1992) (noting that historical Bureau of Prisons’
Health Services Manual, § 6803, provided for continuation of hormone therapy to 
individuals with gender dysphoria). Initial BOP policy, dating back to at least 1992,
1 Gender dysphoria is a serious medical condition characterized by the incongruence between 
one’s gender identity and sex assigned at birth causing clinically significant distress. 
Supp.App.106a–07a. The diagnosis of gender dysphoria is described in the American 
Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (“DSM”). 
Supp.App.106a. Without treatment, gender dysphoria can cause depression, anxiety, selfharm, and suicidality, and can impair a person’s ability to function in all aspects of life. 
Supp.App.107a.

6
was to maintain the treatment people were receiving prior to incarceration, while 
permitting BOP medical staff to make “progressive or regressive treatment changes” 
if such changes were “approved by the [Bureau of Prisons] Medical Director prior to 
implementation.” Id. A 2005 policy continued that approach, ensuring individuals 
prescribed hormone therapy continued receiving such treatment while in custody.2
In 2010, BOP issued a memorandum establishing that hormone therapy could 
be initiated in custody if BOP healthcare providers determined it was “medically 
indicated” based on an individualized evaluation. See supra n.2. Six years later, BOP 
issued clinical guidance, which continued to provide for hormone therapy when 
clinically indicated and gave healthcare providers more guidance on the treatment 
protocols for gender dysphoria.3 In 2017, BOP released its Transgender Offender 
Manual, which further formalized the policy and provided for social transition 
accommodations in addition to hormone therapy. See Supp.App.10a–11a.
The Transgender Offender Manual also established a decision-making body 
called the Transgender Executive Council, which included the senior psychologist, 
psychiatrist, security expert, and medical administrator in BOP. Supp.App.11a–12a. 
At the same time, BOP’s Health Services Division created a Transgender Clinical Care

medical providers. Supp.App.12a. BOP has updated the Transgender Offender Manual
and clinical guidance, most recently in 2022 and 2023, respectively. See Supp.App.26a, 
41a.
BOP developed its gender dysphoria clinical guidance based on a wide variety of 
sources including the Endocrine Society, the University of California San Franciso 
School of Medicine, the World Health Organization, and the World Professional 
Association for Transgender Health (“WPATH”). App.160a, App.165a (Declaration of

Supp.App.2a, 4a–5a, 258a–59a, 267a–68a (former senior BOP psychologist describing 
her experience overseeing care of transgender people in custody and noting her 
involvement in the development of policy regarding their care); Supp.App.33a 
(Transgender Offender Manual relying on “individualized assessment” of the patient 
4 Half a century of research and clinical experience from health providers across the United 
States and around the world have demonstrated that the treatment BOP has provided for 
over 30 years is highly effective treatment for gender dysphoria. See Supp.App.103a, 107a, 
112a–13a, 163a. It is therefore widely accepted in the medical community and supported by 
every major American medical professional association. Supp.App.167a. Moreover, hormone

the testes. See Supp.App.193a–96a, 198a–99a, 200a–01a, 203a–04a.

8
“by institution medical staff” to provide “[h]ormone therapy or other medical 
treatment”).
II. EXECUTIVE ORDER 14168 AND BOP’S IMPLEMENTING 
MEMORANDA
On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an EO declaring that “[f]ederal 
funds shall not be used to promote gender ideology,” defined as “the false claim that 
males can identify as and thus become women and vice versa.” App.1a–2a. The EO also
directed the Attorney General to ensure that BOP “revises its policies concerning 
medical care to be consistent with this order” and to “ensure that no Federal funds are 
expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming 
an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” App.3a.
One month after the EO, BOP issued memoranda implementing the EO. BOP’s
first memorandum prohibited the use of appropriated funds to purchase “any items 
that align with transgender ideology” and prohibited any requests for clothing that did 
not “align with an inmate’s biological sex.” App.5a–6a. A second memorandum 
provided that no BOP funds “are to be expended for any medical procedure, treatment, 
or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite 
sex.” App.7a. The EO was the government’s sole provided rationale for the 
implementing memoranda. App.5a, 7a.
III. THE LAWSUIT AND THE INITIAL PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION
Following the EO (and without any stated clinical basis), BOP began moving 
forward with the termination of treatment that Respondents Alishea Kingdom, Jas 
Kapule, and Solo Nichols had been receiving for years. Despite the disagreement of

9
Ms. Kingdom’s BOP doctor, BOP stopped providing hormone therapy to Ms. Kingdom,
who had been receiving this treatment from BOP doctors since 2016. The deprivation 
of her medication caused Ms. Kingdom “incapacitating” distress, panic attacks, and 
suicidal thoughts. Supp.App.271a, 272a–73a. Respondents Jas Kapule and Solo 
Nichols—who had also been treated with hormone therapy for several years—were told 
that their treatment would be discontinued, and a BOP doctor began tapering 
Mr. Nichols off his medication. Supp.App.281a, 282a–83a; Supp.App.291a–92a. 
Mr. Nichols’s BOP psychologist apologized to him and said this is not the decision she 
would have made. Supp.App.282a. BOP also withheld social transition 
accommodations from all Respondents. Supp.App.272a, 283a, 292a.
In March 2025, Respondents challenged BOP’s implementation of the EO under 
the Eighth and Fifth Amendments to the Constitution, the APA, and the Rehabilitation 
Act of 1973. Refiled Compl. ¶¶ 96–137, Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691 (D.D.C. Mar. 
10, 2025), Dkt. No. 4-1. Respondents moved for class certification and a preliminary 
injunction based on their Eighth Amendment and APA claims.
On June 3, 2025, the district court granted both motions. The court certified a 
class of all persons who are or will be in the custody of BOP facilities and who have or 
will have a diagnosis of gender dysphoria. It then preliminarily enjoined BOP from 
enforcing its memoranda implementing the EO, concluding that Respondents were 
likely to succeed on their APA claim. Order 1–2, Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691 
(D.D.C. June 3, 2025), Dkt. No. 68. The court subsequently granted Respondents’ 
motions to renew the preliminary injunction pursuant to the PLRA. 18 U.S.C.

10
§ 3626(a)(2); Orders, Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691 (D.D.C. Aug. 20, 2025, Nov. 17, 
2025, Feb. 12, 2026, May 26, 2026), Dkt. Nos. 79, 96, 114, 202.
The government did not appeal the initial preliminary injunction. Nor did the 
government appeal the August 20, 2025, November 17, 2025, or February 12, 2026, 
renewals of the preliminary injunction.5
IV. BOP’S PROGRAM STATEMENT AND ADMINISTRATIVE RECORD
On February 19, 2026, BOP issued the Program Statement. It mirrors the
language used in the EO and implementing memoranda, stating that its intent “is for 
federal funds to not be expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the 
purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex to the 
maximum extent permitted by law.” App.16a. BOP stated it was adopting this policy
“independently of” the EO. The Program Statement also states that BOP will comply 
with the EO absent a court order prohibiting compliance. App.13a.
Like the implementing memoranda, the Program Statement categorically 
prohibits hormone therapy and social transition accommodations as treatments for
gender dysphoria, regardless of an individual patient’s medical need or the 
recommendations of BOP’s medical providers. App.14a. For people already receiving 
such treatment, the policy requires that they be tapered off. App.14a–15a. Under the 
Program Statement, if someone currently has social transition accommodations, BOP

11
will, “when practicable, remove or confiscate” them. App.15a.
The Program Statement provides for psychotherapy as a treatment for gender 
dysphoria and directs that psychotropic medication be considered “to determine if its 
use may alleviate the symptoms of [gender dysphoria].” App.13a–14a.
The administrative record for the Program Statement includes a memorandum 
(“the AR memo”) which puts forward BOP’s stated reasoning for its policy change. 
According to the AR memo, BOP concluded categorically that the banned treatments
were not medically necessary and that providing this care raises security and prison 
administration concerns. App.42a, 50a. The AR memo states that “[i]n evaluating its 
policies on gender dysphoria, BOP considered the relevant issues, factors, information, 
and sources, including conducting extensive reviews of existing research, medical 
expert opinions, medical journals, national media reports, recent medical studies, state 
correctional policies, BOP’s prior policies, and pertinent case law.” App.31a. It cites 
extensively to the opinions of Dr. Kristopher Kaliebe, a psychiatrist with virtually no 
experience treating patients with gender dysphoria and whom BOP retained as an 
expert specifically for this litigation. App.175a.
Nothing in the administrative record contains any discussion of BOP’s own 
experience providing hormone therapy for over three decades and social transition 
accommodations for the past ten years. The administrative record does not include any 
statements by BOP healthcare officials who oversee the provision of this treatment or 
by BOP doctors who continue to deem this care clinically indicated for the patients for 
whom they prescribe it. The administrative record is also silent about the impact of

12
this treatment on the health of patients who have been receiving this care and does not 
include or refer to any BOP medical records or other BOP clinical data about the 
Respondents or other Class members. 
Similarly, at no point does the administrative record address whether any of the 
security or administrative concerns mentioned in the AR memo materialized during 
the more than 30 years the care at issue has been provided. The administrative record 
also does not include any discussion of whether there are measures available to provide 
this care safely, as BOP does with other medical treatments that pose security issues
such as methadone treatment for opioid use disorder. See Supp.App.260a–62a. The
administrative record contains no incident reports showing there were any security 
issues that arose from providing this care; nor is there discussion or mention of any 
such incidents.
V. THE UPDATED PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION AND PROCEEDINGS 
BELOW
Respondents filed a supplemental complaint challenging the Program 
Statement and moved for an updated preliminary injunction to enjoin the Program 
Statement. See Mot. for Prelim. Inj., Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691 (D.D.C. Apr. 
29, 2026), Dkt. No. 179; Suppl. Compl., Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691 (D.D.C. Apr. 
30, 2026), Dkt. No. 182. In support of their motion, Respondents submitted their own 
declarations and three expert declarations. In opposition, the government filed 
excerpts of the administrative record and a declaration from BOP Medical Director 
Dr. Elizabete Stahl that was not part of the administrative record. App.149a.
Respondents submitted rebuttal expert declarations with their reply.

13
The district court issued a preliminary injunction barring BOP from enforcing 
the Program Statement and requiring BOP to continue providing treatment for gender 
dysphoria in accordance with its pre-EO policy. App.169a. Applying settled APA 
precedents, the court determined that Respondents are likely to succeed on their APA 
arbitrary-and-capricious claim on three interrelated but independent bases: (1) BOP 
did not consider its own prior experience providing the care banned by the Program 
Statement; (2) the Program Statement is objectively unreasonable in light of the 
evidence before BOP; and (3) the reasons given for the Program Statement were 
pretextual and the Program Statement was reverse engineered to implement the EO. 
App.187a–95a.
On June 22, 2026, the government appealed the updated preliminary injunction 
and moved for a stay pending appeal in the district court. Mot. to Stay the Prelim. Inj., 
Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691 (D.D.C. June 22, 2026), Dkt. No. 222. The district

ARGUMENT
A stay pending appeal is reserved for “extraordinary circumstances.” Williams 
v. Zbaraz, 442 U.S. 1309, 1311 (1979) (Stevens, J., in chambers). To succeed on its

on the merits,” that it will be “irreparably injured” without a stay, that a stay will not 
“substantially injure the other parties,” and that a stay furthers “the public interest.” 
Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 434 (2009). The government must also show “a 
reasonable probability” that the Court will grant certiorari on the question presented 
in its stay application. Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam).
The government fails at each step.

The government is also unlikely to succeed on its arguments that the district

these arguments by failing to make them in the district court. App.209a. The 
government itself admits that it made these arguments for the first time in its motion 
for a stay in the D.C. Circuit. Appl.32. Neither that court nor this Court are courts of

This Court should not be the first to decide these arguments, and particularly not on a 
rushed stay application. 
2. Even if the government had presented these arguments to the district 
court, they fail on the merits. The government’s argument that the district court did 
not make specific findings under the PLRA is wrong several times over. First, the 
government relies solely on Hoffer v. Secretary, Fla. Dep’t of Corr., 973 F.3d 1263 (11th 
Cir. 2020). Appl. 30. But Hoffer concerned 18 U.S.C. § 3626(a)(1), which applies to 
permanent injunctions—not § 3626(a)(2), which applies to preliminary injunctions like 
the one here. The PLRA clearly applies different requirements for temporary and 
permanent relief and Congress’s choice must be respected. See, e.g., Sebelius v. Auburn 
Reg’l Med. Ctr., 568 U.S. 145, 156 (2013) (“Congress’s use of certain language in one 
part of the statute and different language in another can indicate that different 
meanings were intended.”) (citation modified). 
Second, neither section of the PLRA requires the district court to make 
“particularized findings.” Appl.30–31. Section 3626(a)(2)—the provision applicable 
here—does not speak to the sort of findings a court must make. Instead, the provision 
requires that preliminary injunctive relief be “narrowly drawn, extend no further than

32
necessary to correct the harm the court finds requires preliminary relief, and be the 
least intrusive means necessary to correct that harm.” 18 U.S.C. § 3626(a)(2). While 
Section 3626(a)(1)—the provision on which the government erroneously relies—
requires the district court to “find[]” that the relief is “narrowly drawn, extends no 
further than necessary to correct the violation of the Federal right, and is the least 
intrusive means necessary to correct the violation of the Federal right,” the statute’s 
text does not impose a further requirement that a court make “particularized findings,” 
as the government now contends. This Court “has rejected every attempt to deviate 
from the PLRA’s textual mandate,” Ross v. Blake, 578 U.S. 632, 633 (2016), because
“crafting and imposing” “rules [that] are not required by the PLRA . . . exceeds the 
proper limits on the judicial role,” Jones v. Bock, 549 U.S. 199, 203 (2007). See also 
Brown v. Plata, 563 U.S. 493, 531 (2011) (imposing no “particularized findings” 
requirement). 
Third, and most importantly, the district court here did make particularized 
findings. App.170a, 206a–07a. Other than empty accusations that the district court 
relied on conclusory statements, the government does not identify any findings the 
district court failed to make before issuing interim relief that is narrowly tailored to 
address the irreparable harm that would result from BOP’s new policy. Appl.30. That 
the findings were “nearly identical” to the court’s findings in previous orders enjoining 
BOP’s implementation of the EO, Appl.30, is to be expected—the harms and scope of 
relief required to prevent those harms are “nearly identical.” Notably, the government 
did not take issue with the court’s “nearly identical” prior findings and did not appeal

33
those injunctions. See supra at 10.
3. The district court also comported with all of the PLRA’s other 
requirements, including the least-restrictive rule, by ordering relief that is “narrowly 
drawn, extends no further than necessary to correct the harm that the Court finds 
requires preliminary relief, and is the least intrusive means necessary to correct that 
harm.” App.206a (citing 18 U.S.C. § 3626(a)(2)). It determined that the injunction 
“extends no further than necessary to correct the harm that requires this preliminary 
relief” because it only “prevents the application of the Program Statement.” Id. The 
preliminary injunction does not require BOP to provide treatment to all class members, 
but rather maintains the pre-EO status quo, which permitted BOP medical personnel 
to administer such care to those individuals for whom it is clinically indicated. 
App.205a–06a. The district court also carefully considered “any adverse impact on 
public safety or on the operation of the criminal justice system caused by this relief” 
and found that no such adverse impacts “will result from maintaining the status quo 
of the class members’ medical care while this litigation proceeds.” App.206–07a. 
The government’s argument to the contrary misunderstands the nature of the 
preliminary injunction. The government argues first that the district court should have 
enjoined only those portions of the Program Statement concerning hormone therapy 
and social transition accommodations. Appl.30–32. But the scope of the preliminary 
injunction is properly tailored to the evidence in the record demonstrating that the 
entire Program Statement likely is arbitrary and capricious. Supra Argument § I.A. 
The district court appropriately stayed the Program Statement under 5 U.S.C. § 705,

34
App.205a, which permits courts to “issue all necessary and appropriate process to 
postpone the effective date of an agency action” “[o]n such conditions as may be 
required and to the extent necessary to prevent irreparable injury.” 5 U.S.C. § 705. And 
where a court finds a prison policy unlawful, the PLRA permits enjoining the policy in 
its entirety. E.g., Fields v. Smith, 653 F.3d 550, 558–59 (7th Cir. 2011) (affirming
injunction of policy banning gender-affirming care); Crawford v. Clarke, 578 F.3d 39, 
43–44 (1st Cir. 2009) (affirming injunction of policy restricting religious practice). 
The government next tries a different attack on the scope of the relief granted, 
arguing that the preliminary injunction is not the least restrictive measure because 
not all class members may require hormone therapy or social transition 
accommodations to treat gender dysphoria. Appl.32–33. But that attack fails for two 
reasons. First, it is an untimely challenge to the district court’s class certification 
decision; the government never appealed that decision, and their time to do so has long 
passed. Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(f); Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, 586 U.S. 188, 193–94
(2019) (Rule 23(f)’s deadline may not be equitably tolled). 
Second, the government’s contention misses the point: Class members have 
gender dysphoria diagnoses and are injured because the Program Statement 
“precludes medical professionals from prescribing a gender-affirming treatment plan 
based on an inmate’s unique needs” and therefore “puts all class members at risk of 
being denied medically necessary care.” App.199a. The preliminary injunction thus 
“provide[s] relief to each member of the class,” Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 
338, 360 (2011), because it allows everyone in BOP custody with gender dysphoria to

35
be afforded an individualized assessment in which hormone therapy and social 
transition accommodations are considered as potential treatments if clinically 
indicated. Because the Program Statement imposed a categorical ban, permitting no 
one to be treated with hormone therapy or social transition accommodations, the 
remedy here is “proportional to the scope of the violation.” Brown, 563 U.S. at 531. It 
“extend[s] no further than necessary” because it does not require BOP to provide care 
to people who do not need it. Id. at 531–33 (rejecting claim that injunctive relief was 
overbroad in violation of the PLRA).
II. THE REMAINING STAY FACTORS FAVOR RESPONDENTS.
Given that government has failed to show it is likely to prevail on the merits, 
the Court can “start and stop with the first [stay] factor.” Trump v. Cook, 609 U.S. 528, 
535 (2026). But the remaining factors also weigh strongly against a stay.
A. The Government Will Not Suffer Irreparable Harm Absent A Stay.
To obtain a stay, applicants must demonstrate that they “will be irreparably 
injured” in its absence. Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 426 (2009); Ruckelshaus v. 
Monsanto Co., 463 U.S. 1315, 1317 (1983) (Blackmun, J., in chambers) (“An applicant’s 
likelihood of success on the merits need not be considered, however, if the applicant 
fails to show irreparable injury from the denial of the stay” (citing Whalen v. Roe, 423 
U.S. 1313, 1317–18 (1975) (Marshall, J., in chambers)). The government has failed to 
demonstrate any such irreparable harm.
The government’s claim of irreparable harm absent emergency relief is difficult 
to take seriously given that it did not appeal or seek a stay of the court’s preliminary

36
injunction issued over a year ago—which, just like the injunction at issue here, 
maintained the longstanding status quo permitting BOP medical staff to treat people 
with hormone therapy and social transition accommodations for gender dysphoria. The 
government has no explanation for why it is suddenly so urgent for it to rescind this 
health care and upend a three-decade status quo. See Ruckelshaus, 463 U.S. at 1317
(denying stay where the applicant “ha[d] not been particularly expeditious in seeking 
a stay”). In fact, the government failed to even raise any claim of irreparable injury 
before the district court, thus forfeiting the argument now.
But separate from the government’s forfeiture and inexcusable delay, its claim 
of irreparable harm is meritless. Its contention that it “is irreparably harmed by an 
improper intrusion by a federal court into the workings of a coordinate branch of the 
[g]overnment,” Appl.35 (citation modified)—rests on the false premise that the court’s 
decision was “improper.” As explained above, supra Argument § I.A, it was not. 
Moreover, the government suffers no injury by being required to continue to 
provide care that they have been providing for decades—and which BOP’s own 
healthcare providers continue to recommend for patients while this case proceeds. The 
preliminary injunction does not impose any “administrative burden” on BOP, let alone 
a “considerable” one. INS v. Legalization Assistance Project of L.A. Cnty. Fed’n of Labor, 
510 U.S. 1301, 1305 (1993) (O’Connor, J., in chambers). 
Besides its arguments that it suffers irreparable harm by continuing to offer the 
health care that hundreds of individuals rely on, the government makes vague 
references to “security and administration concerns” and “scientific uncertainty” of

37
gender-affirming care. Appl.35–36. But the government does not explain how such 
indefinite and speculative interests would cause any sort of “ongoing and concrete 
harm” to the government, Maryland v. King, 567 U.S. 1301, 1303 (2012). “Simply 
showing some possibility of irreparable injury fails to satisfy” the standard for a stay. 
Nken, 556 U.S. at 434–35 (citation modified).
Thus, the government’s own actions belie any claim of irreparable harm that 
would warrant this Court’s extraordinary intervention pending the resolution of the 
appeal. Order 1, Kingdom v. Trump, No. 26-5236 (D.C. Cir. Sep. 22, 2026), Dkt. No.
2194449 (appeal to be fully briefed by December 23, 2026).
B. Respondents Will Be Irreparably Harmed If the Status Quo Is 
Upended By a Stay.
“[T]he traditional stay inquiry calls for assessing the harm to the opposing party 
and weighing the public interest. These factors merge when the Government is the 
opposing party.” Nken, 556 U.S. at 435. The harm to Respondents in the event of the 
stay would be immediate and catastrophic—they will have ongoing medical treatment 
withdrawn. The record clearly demonstrates that this will lead to serious adverse 
health consequences. 
Respondents have already experienced negative physical and mental health 
consequences when BOP previously withdrew their hormone therapy temporarily in 
response to the EO. As discussed above, supra Statement § III, Respondents
experienced worsening gender dysphoria and endured symptoms including depression, 
panic attacks, hot flashes, thoughts of self-harm, and suicidal ideation. Respondents 
have grave fears they will experience more of the same—and worse—if the government

38
permanently removes the gender-affirming treatment they rely on for their health. 
Supp.App.277a, 287a, 297a.
Respondents’ sworn declarations are supported by those of medical experts, who 
explain that withdrawal of hormone therapy will lead to physical changes that 
exacerbate gender dysphoria, causing substantial distress and associated mental 
health consequences. See Supp.App.193a; Supp.App.205a (“In my experience with 
patients who had to discontinue hormone therapy because of loss of insurance, they 
experienced significant distress as their bodies began to misalign with their gender 
identity; in some cases, this caused severe functional impairment where patients were 
no longer able to function at work.”). Those consequences can be extremely severe, as 
patients who are denied hormone therapy can suffer from increased depression, 
anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-harm, including attempts to remove their own 
genitals or breasts. Supp.App.114a–16a (discussing the impacts of delayed or denied 
gender affirming care).9 Though the government repeatedly tries to dismiss the risk of 
self-harm by characterizing it as an attempt to obtain “rewards” or “concessions” from 
prison officials, Appl.10, 24, such assertions grossly mischaracterize the nature of the 
medical condition and the depth of harm. Untreated gender dysphoria carries a highrisk of suicidality and self-harm for people both in and outside of custody.
Supp.App.107a, 114a, 115a–16a.
The government’s only response is its conclusory assertion that “BOP found that

hormone interventions in general . . . are not ‘medically necessary,’” Appl.36, which is 
undermined by the fact that its own medical staff have prescribed and continue to 
prescribe these treatments to Respondents and other Class members only after 
determining they were clinically indicated. Supp.App.41a.
The government asserts that BOP will offer psychotherapy and psychotropic 
medications as “appropriate, individualized treatment.” Appl.36. But such “treatment” 
categorically overrides the individualized determinations that previously have been 
made by BOP’s medical providers and offers only treatments that have not been shown 
to alleviate gender dysphoria. See supra Statement § I. Ultimately, the public interest 
is served by maintaining the status quo and preventing these predictable and 
irreparable harms to Respondents and the Class.
The government contends that Respondents have not demonstrated irreparable 
harm on a class-wide basis, but as already noted, supra at 34–35, this mischaracterizes 
the preliminary relief ordered by the district court. The Program Statement would 
cause irreparable harm to all members of the Class because it imposes a categorical 
ban on hormone therapy and social transition accommodations without regard to 
individualized need for those interventions, putting all class members at risk of being 
denied the care they need. The preliminary injunction does not require BOP to provide 
any intervention to people who do not need it; it merely prevents BOP from 
categorically withholding care that its own doctors deem appropriate for certain 
patients.

III. THE CASE IS NOT WORTHY OF CERTIORARI IN THIS POSTURE.
The stay application should also be denied because certiorari is not warranted 
in this posture. Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010).
The district court issued a fact-bound, preliminary order based on its 
determination that BOP’s sudden reversal of its own longstanding policy of providing 
hormone therapy and social transition accommodations based on individual 
assessments of clinical need was arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 705 (providing 
that district court may “postpone” agency action “to preserve status or rights pending 
conclusion of the review proceedings”). The standard for arbitrary-and-capricious 
review under the APA is “well-worn,” Wages & White Lion, 604 U.S.at 567, and does 
not merit this Court’s review, particularly in this “interlocutory posture,” which “is a 
factor counseling against this Court’s review at this time.” Nat’l Football League v. 
Ninth Inning, Inc., 592 U.S. 1081, 1082 (2020) (Kavanaugh, J., statement respecting 
denial of certiorari). The government’s application concerns only Respondents’ APA 
arbitrary-and-capricious challenge and does not address Respondents’ other claims 
yet to be fully litigated in the district court. The resolution of the issue presented in 
the government’s application would not be dispositive of this case, which further 
counsels against this Court’s review. Halbert v. Michigan, 545 U.S. 605, 632 (2005)
(Thomas, J., dissenting) (“[T]his Court would be unlikely to grant certiorari in a case 
to announce a rule that could not alter the case’s disposition”).
CONCLUSION
The Court should deny the government’s application for a stay.
